1163.title: Weak hadith and virtue
1163.hook: scholars differ on using weak hadith for encouragement, never for law
1163.howItsDone: Muslim teachers differ on whether weak reports may be recited to encourage good deeds; those who allow it often signal the doubt with wording such as "it is reported", and weak reports are not used to establish law.

segments.voice: Yesterday: memorizing chains, the names and the words held together, and your line: by heart.

A card on a fridge door, held up by a magnet. On it, a gentle saying about kindness to neighbors, and underneath: the Prophet ﷺ. Nobody in the house remembers where the card came from. Is the saying sound? Weak? Made up by someone with good intentions? Suppose a report is weak, but all it does is urge people toward something good. May it be used at all? Scholars have answered that differently, and both answers are worth hearing. Today: weak hadith and virtue.
screen: `A CARD ON THE FRIDGE.` → `WHERE DID IT COME FROM?` → `WEAK, BUT URGING GOOD?`

segments.voice: First, what weak means. A weak report, da'if in Arabic, isn't necessarily false. The chain or the text fell short: a narrator with a poor memory, a gap where a name should be. The critics simply can't vouch for it. Then, the line drawn around law. In this discussion, weak reports were kept away from questions of what is permitted and what is forbidden; law needed firmer ground. Then the disagreement. Some scholars allowed a weak report to be mentioned to encourage a good deed that already stands on sound texts: giving charity, being patient, remembering Allah. Tradition says they set conditions. The report must not be very weak. The deed must already be grounded elsewhere. And the speaker must not claim with certainty that the Prophet said it. Other scholars refused weak reports altogether, even for encouragement, holding that the sound reports give more than enough. Last, why both sides cared so much. In the introduction to his Sahih, Imam Muslim records a report that whoever narrates something from the Prophet that he sees to be a lie is one of the liars. And Sahih al-Bukhari carries the Prophet's warning against anyone who lies about him on purpose. So both sides guard the same thing: one by keeping doubtful reports at arm's length, clearly labeled, the other by keeping them out of the room. You can hear the care in the wording some scholars used: not the Prophet said, but it is reported. A small change of words, and an honest one.
screen: `WEAK IS NOT THE SAME AS FALSE.` · `KEPT AWAY FROM LAW.` · `SOME ALLOWED IT, WITH CONDITIONS.` · `BOTH SIDES GUARD HIS WORDS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a line you've repeated as someone else's words: a quote you posted, a saying you credit to a parent, a teacher, a prophet. Do you actually know where it came from? Without scolding yourself, rest a moment in the small gap between he said and it's said that he said.

Weak hadith and virtue. Whether a report the critics can't vouch for may be used to encourage good deeds: some scholars allowed it with conditions, some refused, and they kept it away from law. Today's word.
Your line: careful with the weak. Not the Prophet said, but it is reported. See you tomorrow.

1164.title: The forty tradition
1164.hook: scholars gathered forty hadith, hoping for a reward promised in a report
1164.howItsDone: Muslim students learn and memorize al-Nawawi's forty, line by line with a teacher, and other scholars have compiled forties of their own on many subjects.

segments.voice: Yesterday: weak reports and good deeds, allowed by some scholars with conditions, refused by others, and your line: careful with the weak.

Here is a book that begins by admitting something. In the introduction to his little collection of forty hadith, the scholar al-Nawawi mentions a report: whoever preserves forty hadith about the religion for the Prophet's community will be raised among the people of knowledge. He says that promise is what moved scholars before him to gather forties of their own. And right there, in his own introduction, al-Nawawi says the report is weak. Yesterday's question, sitting on the first pages of a real book. So why write it at all? Today: the forty tradition.
screen: `A BOOK THAT ADMITS SOMETHING.` → `PRESERVE FORTY.` → `AND THE REPORT IS WEAK.`

segments.voice: The report promises that someone who preserves forty hadith for the community, on matters of the religion, will be raised with the scholars. Al-Nawawi notes that it comes by many routes and that the hadith critics agree it is weak. He also names scholars before him who gathered forties anyway, on belief, on law, on renouncing the world, on good manners, each with a different aim. But he doesn't rest his book on the weak report. He points instead to sound ones: the Prophet's instruction that whoever is present should pass his words on to whoever is absent, and the prayer for the one who hears his words and conveys them as he heard them. That's the prayer from the day on memorizing chains, now holding up a whole book. Next, what he gathered. Not forty on a single subject, but sayings he considered foundations, each one, as he described it, a great principle of the religion. His collection opens with the report on intentions, the line that also opens Bukhari's Sahih. The second is the hadith of Jibril: Islam, iman and ihsan. And religion is sincere counsel, memorized two days back, has its place too. Last, why forty. The book never claims the number is holy. It's a number a person can carry: a book built to fit inside a memory, learned, recited, taught line by line, small enough to take anywhere and deep enough to keep opening.
screen: `THE HOPE IN A WEAK REPORT.` · `HIS FOOTING: SOUND REPORTS.` · `FORTY FOUNDATIONS, NOT ONE TOPIC.` · `A BOOK THAT FITS IN A MEMORY.`

Then let a question rest, without a quick answer: if you could carry forty sayings anywhere, which would you want in your pocket first?
The forty tradition. Collections of forty hadith, gathered in hope of a promise from a weak report, and grounded by al-Nawawi on sound reports about passing the Prophet's words on. Today's word.
Your line: forty to carry. Two of them are already yours. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1165.title: Hadith commentary
1165.hook: scholars like Ibn Hajar wrote vast commentaries
1165.howItsDone: Students of hadith read a collection alongside a commentary, such as Ibn Hajar's Fath al-Bari on Bukhari or al-Nawawi's commentary on Muslim, usually with a teacher who explains the commentary in turn.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the forty tradition, al-Nawawi's book built to fit inside a memory, and your line: forty to carry.

How much can be said about one sentence? Not a summary of it. An explanation. What each word means. Who carried it, and from whom. How another version words it. What scholars drew from it, and where they parted ways. Put all that under a line you could say in one breath, and it runs on for pages. The scholar Ibn Hajar wrote one of these on the whole of Sahih al-Bukhari, a vast work, saying by saying. That surrounding writing has a name. Today: sharh.
screen: `ONE SENTENCE.` → `EXPLAINED, NOT SUMMARIZED.` → `IBN HAJAR, SAYING BY SAYING.`

segments.voice: Sharh means explanation: a commentary written on a hadith collection, one report at a time. Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani wrote Fath al-Bari on Bukhari. Al-Nawawi, the compiler of yesterday's forty, wrote one on Sahih Muslim. And the forties got commentaries of their own. So what does a commentator do? Take a line you already hold: actions are only by intentions. He starts with the words. What is an intention, exactly? A passing thought, or a settled direction of the heart? Then the chain: who carried it, and from whom. Then the rest of the text, because the hadith doesn't stop where the slogan does. In its fuller versions in Bukhari it goes on: whoever emigrated for Allah and His Messenger, his emigration is for Allah and His Messenger, and whoever emigrated for something of this world, or to marry a woman, his emigration is for what he emigrated for. Read whole, it's about one outward act carrying two very different inner journeys. Then the questions of practice: does an act of worship count without an intention behind it? Here commentators lay out the views of earlier scholars, say who held them, and weigh them. The saying sits in the center. The commentator stands around it, quoting others, disagreeing politely, admitting where he's unsure. The aim isn't to replace the Prophet's words but to keep them from being misread. Ibn Hajar even asks why al-Bukhari opened his book with this report, and one answer given is that the author was setting his own intention right before the work began.
screen: `SHARH: AN EXPLANATION.` · `FIRST THE WORDS, THEN THE CHAIN.` · `THE REST OF THE HADITH.` · `THE SAYING IN THE CENTER.`

segments.voice: Take the line, actions are only by intentions, and pick one word from it: actions, or only, or intentions. Hold it the way a commentator would: what does it mean, and what would the line lose without it? Then let the questions go and rest with the whole line on the breath.
Sharh. An explanation, a commentary written around a hadith collection, saying by saying, like Ibn Hajar's on Bukhari. Today's word.
Your line: explained for us. The saying stays in the center. Until tomorrow.

1166.title: Reading hadith today
1166.hook: reading hadith with its context and a teacher
1166.howItsDone: Muslims who study hadith read the collections with a teacher, in a class or circle, who explains each report's setting, its other versions, and how scholars have understood it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sharh, the commentary that keeps a saying from being misread, and your line: explained for us.

Help your brother, whether he is an oppressor or oppressed. Stop the sentence there and it sounds like a call to back your own side no matter what. The people who first heard it seem to have stumbled too, because in Sahih al-Bukhari someone asks the Prophet ﷺ: helping him when he's wronged, that we understand, but how do we help him when he's the oppressor? And the answer turns the whole thing around. By stopping him from oppressing. Half a hadith, heard alone, pointed the opposite way from the whole. Today: reading hadith today.
screen: `HELP YOUR BROTHER.` → `HOW, IF HE'S THE OPPRESSOR?` → `BY STOPPING HIM.`

segments.voice: First, the whole text. Reports travel now as screenshots and captions, trimmed to fit. A basic habit of hadith study is the one you just heard: find the full report, question and answer, before deciding what it says. Second, the setting. Scholars paid attention to the occasion of a saying, sabab al-wurud: who asked, what had just happened, who was being spoken to. When Abdullah ibn Amr was told that his body had a right over him, it was because he had been fasting every day and standing in prayer every night. Lift that line out of its story and it can be made to say almost anything. Third, the neighbors. A single report sits among others on the same subject, and among the verses of the Qur'an. Jurists read them side by side, and the schools of law sometimes reached different conclusions from the same texts. That's where this year turns next. Fourth, the person. In the introduction to his Sahih, Imam Muslim records a saying of the early scholar Muhammad ibn Sirin: this knowledge is religion, so look carefully at whom you take your religion from. The chain didn't stop when the books were finished. Students went on reading the collections aloud in front of teachers, who could say: this word means this, that report explains this one, here the scholars differ. That's still how this tradition reads hadith at its most careful: the words, the setting, the other texts, and someone who has walked the road before you.
screen: `FIND THE WHOLE REPORT.` · `SABAB AL-WURUD: THE SETTING.` · `READ IT BESIDE ITS NEIGHBORS.` · `LOOK AT WHOM YOU LEARN FROM.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a hadith you've heard quoted, maybe on a screen, and put today's questions to it gently: is that the whole of it, who was being spoken to, what else is said on this? Notice which ones you can't answer. Then think of one person you could ask, an imam, a teacher, a friend who studies, and hold their face in mind for a breath.
Reading hadith today. Taking a report whole, in its setting, beside the other texts, and with someone who has studied it. Today's word.
Your line: with a teacher. The whole report, in its setting, beside its neighbors. One more day, kept.

1167.title: Hadith close
1167.hook: a science built on honesty, memory and travel
1167.howItsDone: Muslims often ask Allah's mercy for the scholars and narrators who carried the hadith, and students of hadith sometimes name their chain of teachers back to the Prophet when they teach.

segments.voice: Yesterday: reading hadith today, whole, in its setting, beside the other texts, and your line: with a teacher.

Every saying in this block arrived the same way. Aisha telling what the Prophet ﷺ did at home. Jibril asking about ihsan. Allah saying, whoever comes walking, I come running. Someone heard each one, held it, and handed it on, and someone else checked the one who handed it on. That's the whole block in a sentence. A science built on honesty, on memory, and on travel. Today the block on hadith comes to a close, and the question is simple: across all those hands, how did the chain hold? Today: hadith close.
screen: `HEARD, HELD, HANDED ON.` → `AND CHECKED.` → `HOW DID THE CHAIN HOLD?`

segments.voice: Walk back down the block, link by link. A hadith: a report of what the Prophet said, did or approved. Sunnah and hadith: the way, carried. Chain and text: who told whom, and the words, tested too. Sound, good, weak: graded with care. Many chains. The science of men: who was he? Scholars on the road for a single report. Fabrications exposed, because they checked. Then the books: Bukhari's sound collection, Muslim's, the four Sunan that complete the six books, the early collections of Malik and Ahmad, and the four books of the Shia with their own science of grading. Then the sacred hadith, Jibril's questions, the women who taught the Sahih, memory, weak reports, the forties, commentary, and reading with a teacher. Three threads run through it all. Honesty: the warnings against lying about the Prophet, taken seriously enough to build a whole craft of checking. Memory: words carried by heart, passed on just as they were heard. Travel: students crossing long distances to sit in front of one narrator. And one thing nobody could see from outside: every link was a person who could have cut a corner, and the narrators the critics trusted were the ones who didn't. So the chain held. Not that every report is sound; this block spent whole days on weak and fabricated ones. What held was the method. Name your source. Test it. Say how sure you are. Tomorrow a new block begins: fiqh and the schools, what scholars built from the Qur'an and these reports.
screen: `LINK BY LINK, THE WHOLE BLOCK.` · `HONESTY, MEMORY, TRAVEL.` · `A PERSON AT EVERY LINK.` · `THE METHOD HELD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one hadith from this block that stayed with you, and walk back along its chain: the person or book you learned it from, the collector who checked it, the narrators before him, the companion who first heard it. You don't need their names, just the line of people, hand to hand. If you pray, ask mercy for them; if you don't, let some thanks go to each pair of hands.
Hadith close. The end of the block on hadith: a science of reports built on honesty, memory and travel, that kept the Prophet's words and checked them, link by link. Today's word.
Your line: the chain held. Hand to hand, all the way to you. The hadith block is done.

1168.title: Shari'ah and fiqh
1168.hook: shari'ah is the path Allah set; fiqh is the scholars' understanding of it
1168.howItsDone: Muslims who want to know how to pray, fast or trade rightly turn to fiqh, the rulings scholars have worked out, often through the books or teachers of one school of law.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the block on hadith, and your line: the chain held. What held was the method: name your source, test it, say how sure.

Two words get used as if they meant the same thing, in headlines and arguments and around dinner tables. Shari'ah. Fiqh. Inside the tradition they aren't the same, and the space between them is where this whole new block lives. One is the path Allah set. The other is the scholars' understanding of that path: written down, argued over, refined, sometimes corrected. A path, and maps of it drawn by careful people. A new block begins today, on fiqh and the schools of law, and it starts by telling the two apart. Today: shari'ah.
screen: `TWO WORDS, NOT ONE.` → `THE PATH.` → `AND THE MAPS OF IT.`

segments.voice: First, shari'ah. The word is in the Qur'an itself. In surah al-Jathiyah, Allah tells the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ that He has set him on a shari'ah, a clear road of the command, and tells him to follow it. So the word names something Allah sets, not something people invent. Second, fiqh, which means understanding. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet says that when Allah wants good for someone, He gives that person understanding of the religion, and the verb there is the verb of fiqh. Fiqh is the scholars' work: reading the Qur'an and the sunnah closely and working out what they ask of a person in prayer, fasting, trade, marriage and the rest of a life. Third, why the difference matters. Muslims hold the shari'ah to come from Allah. Fiqh is human understanding of it, and a scholar can be right or wrong. Bukhari records the Prophet saying that a judge who strives for the right ruling and reaches it has two rewards, and one who strives and misses has one. An honest error, after real effort, is still rewarded. That's part of why there are schools of law, and why their differences can stand side by side. Fourth, the picture. A map is drawn from the land by people who walked it carefully. Good maps can differ in what they show and how. None of them is the land itself. Sunni and Shia scholars both draw these maps, each with their own methods, and this block looks next at the sources they draw from, beginning tomorrow with the Qur'an.
screen: `SHARI'AH: A ROAD ALLAH SETS.` · `FIQH: UNDERSTANDING.` · `TWO REWARDS, OR ONE.` · `THE MAP IS NOT THE LAND.`

segments.voice: Say the two words slowly, one on each breath: shari'ah, the path; fiqh, the understanding, the map. Then take one ordinary act from your day, washing, eating, a kind word, and notice its two layers: the good it aims at, and the careful how-to people have worked out.
Shari'ah. The path Allah set, a word the Qur'an itself uses. Fiqh is the scholars' understanding of it. Today's word.
Your line: the path and the map. The map is not the land. A new block, begun.

strive and rule; an honest error after real effort still earns a reward.

fork.reveal: strive and get it right, two rewards; strive and miss, one. the effort is honored, which is part of why schools can differ with respect.

chat.says: Aren't shari'ah and fiqh just two words for Islamic law?
options: Not quite. Shari'ah is the path Allah set; fiqh is the scholars' understanding of it.
Yes. Both mean the rulings in law books, so neither can ever be wrong.
Not quite. Fiqh comes from Allah; shari'ah is what scholars wrote down.
chat.meaning: Muslims hold the shari'ah to come from Allah. Fiqh is human understanding of it, so a scholar can miss, and an honest miss is still rewarded.

1169.title: The Qur'an as first source
1169.hook: every school begins with the Qur'an
1169.howItsDone: In Islamic law, scholars of the Sunni and Shia schools begin with the Qur'an when working out a ruling, reading its verses of law closely along with their context and purposes.

segments.voice: Yesterday: shari'ah, the path Allah set, and fiqh, the scholars' map of it. Your line: the path and the map.

"O ye who believe! Fasting is prescribed for you, even as it was prescribed for those before you, that ye may ward off (evil)." That's a verse of law, in Pickthall's translation of the Qur'an. Listen to what's packed into one breath. Who it speaks to. A command. A link to people who came before. And a reason. When the schools of law sit down to work out a ruling, this is where they start: with the book, read slowly, phrase by phrase. Today: the Qur'an as first source.
screen: `O YE WHO BELIEVE!` → `A COMMAND, A LINK, A REASON.` → `WHERE THE SCHOOLS START.`

segments.voice: First, why first. Muslims hold the Qur'an to be the speech of Allah, and the schools of law, Sunni and Shia, begin their reasoning there. A well-known report puts it as a scene. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is sending Mu'adh ibn Jabal to Yemen as a judge, and asks how he'll judge. By the Book of Allah, Mu'adh says. And if it isn't there? By the sunnah. And if it isn't there? By my own careful reasoning. Hadith critics have graded that report differently, exactly what the last block taught us to notice. But the order it describes is the order the schools teach. Second, where the law sits. The verses of law aren't gathered into one chapter. They sit among stories, prayers, promises and warnings, so a jurist reads the whole book to find them. Third, the reasons. Like the fasting verse, a ruling often comes with its purpose attached: that ye may ward off evil. Jurists pay close attention to those purposes, and later in this block that attention becomes a method of its own. Fourth, the limits of a single source. The Qur'an commands prayer again and again, but doesn't spell out every movement of it. For that, scholars turn to the second source, tomorrow. And since today ends a week, look back along it: careful with the weak, forty to carry, explained for us, with a teacher, the chain held, the path and the map. Each was about how carefully a tradition handles its sources. Today, the first of them.
screen: `BOOK, THEN SUNNAH, THEN REASONING.` · `LAW AMONG THE STORIES.` · `A RULING WITH ITS REASON.` · `THE BOOK DOESN'T STAND ALONE.`

segments.voice: Read the fasting verse in its pieces, with a breath between each: O ye who believe, who it speaks to; fasting is prescribed for you, the command; even as it was prescribed for those before you, a link to others; that ye may ward off evil, the reason. Then rest on the last piece and let one question sit with you: what is this command for?
The Qur'an as first source. The schools of law begin their reasoning with the Qur'an, its verses of law read closely, reasons and all. Today's word.
screen: `THE QUR'AN AS FIRST SOURCE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the book first. Then the sunnah, then careful reasoning. That's the week, and the first source.

chat.says: If the Qur'an is the first source, why do scholars need anything else?
options: It doesn't spell out everything, like each movement of prayer; for that they turn to the sunnah.
They don't. Every ruling, down to each movement of prayer, is in one chapter of law.
Its verses of law were set aside later in favor of the scholars' own reasoning.
